newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures recovered from an early selloff as a more positive tone returned to the German and U.S. bond markets and domestic investors snapped up bonds at the lows, traders said.

Traders said domestic demand, notably from French insurance companies, served to offset bond sales by non-resident funds and proprietary traders, helping the bond future climb from the day's low of 127.48 to settle at 127.90.
The franc was the main loser, falling to a low of 3.3793 against the mark from 3.3705 on fears the new members of the Bank of France council may push for more aggressive rate cuts.

The fact the two new members, Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard, were both allies of Jacques Chirac and that the bias in the council had shifted away from the more cautious camp headed by Bank of France governor had tarnished the image of the Bank, notably in the eyes of non-resident investors, traders said.
"U.S. clients saw this as a small coup d'etat for Chirac and saw it as a blow for the independence of the bank of France," a trader at a French brokerage said.
He said the fact Senate Chairman Rene Monory and Pierre Mehaignerie, chairman of the National Assembly's finance commission, both criticised the choice left a bad taste.
A futures trader at a large French bank said both PIBOR contracts and the franc had been hit early on by non-resident sales who were cautious ahead of the Bank of France council nominations.
However PIBOR was supported after the announcement by people who believed there would be more aggressive rate cuts now the composition of the council had been changed, he said.
March PIBOR settled down one basis point, resisting the marked decline in the franc which would normally have weighed in the contract, traders said.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris said while the broad lines of French exchange rate policy would remain unchanged the shift in the balance of the council now opened the door to French rates moving below German rates.

"The Bank of France is likely to cut rates faster than before, at least until the German repo (rate) level is reached," he said. "Whether the Bank could try to cut rates below the German level is now an open question whereas before it was not."
The intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates is at 3.15 percent, just above the key German repo rate at three percent.
Most economists have said Trichet would be reluctant to allow rates to pass below German rates.
Call money was unchanged at 3-3/16 5/16 percent.
